meta.provenance: Concepts and trap structures derived from KMF/Gremlin's GRE source set; every stem, all numbers, all options, all explanations and all figures are original. No source text or artwork reproduced. Several single-answer sources were recast into numeric-entry and multiple-answer form, since the Coordinate Geometry source pool skews to MCQ and quantitative comparison.

questions.question:
The figure shows segment PR in the xy-plane. PR is parallel to the y-axis and crosses the x-axis at point Q. Point P is (h, k), where h < 0 and k > 0. If the length of QR is one third the length of PQ, what are the coordinates of R in terms of h and k?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 260" width="320" height="260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#1f2937"/></marker></defs><path d="M70.9 234.0V26.0M100.6 234.0V26.0M130.3 234.0V26.0M160.0 234.0V26.0M189.7 234.0V26.0M219.4 234.0V26.0M249.1 234.0V26.0M56.0 219.1H264.0M56.0 189.4H264.0M56.0 159.7H264.0M56.0 130.0H264.0M56.0 100.3H264.0M56.0 70.6H264.0M56.0 40.9H264.0" stroke="#d7dee8" stroke-width="1" fill="none"/><line x1="56.0" y1="130.0" x2="264.0" y2="130.0" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="160.0" y1="234.0" x2="160.0" y2="26.0" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="260.0" y="146.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">x</text><text x="167.0" y="37.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">y</text><text x="147.0" y="145.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">O</text><line x1="100.6" y1="55.7" x2="100.6" y2="154.8" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="100.6" cy="55.7" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="106.6" y="51.7" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">P (h, k)</text><circle cx="100.6" cy="130.0" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="93.6" y="125.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="end">Q</text><circle cx="100.6" cy="154.8" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="93.6" y="166.8" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="end">R</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Since PR is parallel to the y-axis, every point on it shares P's x-coordinate h, and Q, being on the x-axis, is (h, 0). The length PQ is the vertical gap from k down to 0, which is k. So QR = k/3. Point R lies on the far side of the x-axis from P, which is below it, so R sits k/3 units below the axis at (h, -k/3).
questions.trap: Students compute the length k/3 correctly but write R as (h, k/3), option D, forgetting the sign. R is below the x-axis, so its y-coordinate must be negative.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, line L has equation 7x + 4y = 84. What is the sum of the x-intercept and the y-intercept of L?
questions.explanation: For the x-intercept, set y = 0: 7x = 84, so x = 12. For the y-intercept, set x = 0: 4y = 84, so y = 21. Their sum is 12 + 21 = 33.
questions.trap: Students read the coefficients 7 and 4 as the intercepts and answer 11. The coefficients set the slope; the intercepts come from dividing the constant 84 by each coefficient in turn.

questions.question:
In the xy-plane, the point (k, k) lies on the graph of 0.4x + 0.1y = 15.
Column A: k
Column B: 15
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Because the point has equal coordinates, substitute k for both x and y: 0.4k + 0.1k = 15. The left side collapses to 0.5k, so 0.5k = 15 and k = 30. Since 30 is greater than 15, Column A wins.
questions.trap: Students substitute into only one term, solving 0.4k = 15 to get 37.5 or 0.1k = 15 to get 150. A point on the line y = x makes both variables equal, so both coefficients act on the same k and must be added first.

questions.question:
In the xy-plane, consider the graph of y = (x + 4)/(x - 2).

Which of the following statements are true?

Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The graph crosses the x-axis at x = -4
B. The graph crosses the x-axis at x = 2
C. The graph crosses the y-axis at y = -2
D. The graph is undefined at x = 2
E. The graph crosses the x-axis at x = 4
questions.explanation: A graph meets the x-axis where y = 0, and a fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero while its denominator is not. Setting x + 4 = 0 gives x = -4, and there the denominator is -4 - 2 = -6, safely nonzero, so statement A is true. Statement B fails: at x = 2 the denominator is zero, so the expression is undefined rather than zero, which is exactly what statement D records, making D true. For the y-axis, set x = 0: y = 4/(-2) = -2, so statement C is true. Statement E is false because at x = 4 the value is 8/2 = 4, not 0. Statement F is false because at x = 6 the value is 10/4 = 2.5, not 2.
questions.trap: Statement B catches students who set the whole denominator to zero while hunting for x-intercepts, confusing 'the fraction is zero' with 'the fraction blows up'. A quotient is zero when its top is zero; it is undefined when its bottom is.

questions.question: The figure shows a circle in the xy-plane centered at (-1, -4) and passing through the point (5, 4). What is the circumference of the circle?
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 260" width="320" height="260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#1f2937"/></marker></defs><path d="M62 232V44M97 232V44M132 232V44M202 232V44M237 232V44M272 232V44M44 42H290M44 77H290M44 147H290M44 182H290M44 217H290" stroke="#d7dee8" stroke-width="1" fill="none"/><line x1="44" y1="112" x2="290" y2="112" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="167" y1="236" x2="167" y2="32" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="286" y="128" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">x</text><text x="174" y="44" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">y</text><text x="158" y="99" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="end">O</text><circle cx="160" cy="140" r="70" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="140" x2="202" y2="84" stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="160" cy="140" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="151" y="145" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="end">(-1, -4)</text><circle cx="202" cy="84" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="210" y="80" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">(5, 4)</text></svg>
questions.explanation: The radius is the distance from the center to the point on the circle. The horizontal gap is 5 - (-1) = 6 and the vertical gap is 4 - (-4) = 8, so the radius is sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10. Circumference is 2 pi r, which is 2 pi (10) = 20 pi.
questions.trap: Students compute r^2 = 100 and hand back 100 pi, which is the area, not the circumference. Others stop at the radius and write 10 pi, using pi r rather than 2 pi r.

questions.question:
The figure shows the points (-2, 6) and (-2, -4) in the xy-plane, joined by a dashed segment. The point (x, y), which is not shown in the figure, is equidistant from these two points.
Column A: y
Column B: 1
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 260" width="320" height="260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#1f2937"/></marker></defs><path d="M56.0 234.0V26.0M82.0 234.0V26.0M108.0 234.0V26.0M134.0 234.0V26.0M160.0 234.0V26.0M186.0 234.0V26.0M212.0 234.0V26.0M238.0 234.0V26.0M264.0 234.0V26.0M56.0 221.0H264.0M56.0 195.0H264.0M56.0 169.0H264.0M56.0 143.0H264.0M56.0 117.0H264.0M56.0 91.0H264.0M56.0 65.0H264.0M56.0 39.0H264.0" stroke="#d7dee8" stroke-width="1" fill="none"/><line x1="56.0" y1="143.0" x2="264.0" y2="143.0" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><line x1="160.0" y1="234.0" x2="160.0" y2="26.0" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="260.0" y="159.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">x</text><text x="167.0" y="37.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">y</text><text x="147.0" y="158.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">O</text><circle cx="134.0" cy="65.0" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="127.0" y="69.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="end">(-2, 6)</text><circle cx="134.0" cy="195.0" r="3.5" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="127.0" y="200.0" font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937" text-anchor="end">(-2, -4)</text><line x1="134.0" y1="65.0" x2="134.0" y2="195.0" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: The two fixed points share the x-value -2, so the segment joining them is vertical. The set of points equidistant from the two ends of a segment is its perpendicular bisector, and the perpendicular bisector of a vertical segment is horizontal. It passes through the segment's midpoint, whose y-value is (6 + (-4))/2 = 1. So every equidistant point has y = 1, whatever its x happens to be. Column A is 1, matching Column B.
questions.trap: Students notice that x is completely unpinned and conclude that nothing can be determined, answering D. It is x that is free here, not y: the vertical alignment of the two given points is precisely what locks y to 1.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, a triangle has vertices (0, 2), (c, 2) and (0, 2c), where c is a negative constant. If the area of the triangle is 12, what is the value of c?
questions.explanation: Two vertices share the y-value 2, so that side is horizontal with length |c - 0| = |c|. Two vertices share the x-value 0, so that side is vertical with length |2c - 2| = 2|c - 1|. They meet at (0, 2) at a right angle, so the area is (1/2)(|c|)(2|c - 1|) = |c||c - 1|. Setting that equal to 12 and using c < 0, we have |c| = -c and |c - 1| = 1 - c, giving (-c)(1 - c) = 12, that is c^2 - c - 12 = 0, which factors as (c - 4)(c + 3) = 0. The roots are 4 and -3, and only -3 is negative. Checking: the vertices become (0, 2), (-3, 2) and (0, -6), with legs 3 and 8 and area 12.
questions.trap: Students solve the quadratic and hand back 4, the friendlier-looking root, ignoring the stated condition that c is negative. Both roots give area 12, so the sign condition is the only thing separating them.

questions.question:
In the xy-plane, points R and S have coordinates (6a, -2a) and (-4a, 8a), where a is a nonzero constant.

Which of the following statements are true?

Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The slope of RS is -1
B. The slope of RS depends on the value of a
C. The midpoint of RS is (a, 3a)
D. The midpoint of RS is (1, 3)
E. The length of RS depends on the value of a
F. The length of RS is 10 sqrt(2)
questions.explanation: Compute each quantity and watch what happens to a. The slope of RS is (8a - (-2a))/(-4a - 6a) = 10a/(-10a) = -1: the a cancels top and bottom, so the slope is -1 no matter what a is. That makes statement A true and statement B false. The midpoint averages the coordinates: ((6a + (-4a))/2, (-2a + 8a)/2) = (a, 3a). Averaging is an addition, so a survives, making statement C true and statement D false except in the single case a = 1. The length is sqrt((10a)^2 + (10a)^2) = 10|a|sqrt(2), which grows with |a|, so statement E is true and statement F is false.
questions.trap: Students apply one rule to all three quantities, typically deciding that a always cancels and marking D and F as well. Only the slope is a ratio of two differences, and only there does the common factor divide out; distances and midpoints both scale with a.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, the graph of which of the following equations does NOT intersect the x-axis?
questions.explanation: A graph meets the x-axis at points where y = 0, so substitute y = 0 into each equation and ask whether a real x exists. For y = x - 5, setting y = 0 gives x = 5, so it does cross. For y = x^2 - 4, setting y = 0 gives x^2 = 4 and x = 2 or -2, so it crosses. For y = x^2 + 4, setting y = 0 gives x^2 = -4, which no real number satisfies — this graph never reaches the x-axis, because y is always at least 4. For x = y^2 + 4, setting y = 0 gives x = 4, the perfectly ordinary point (4, 0), so it does cross. For x = y - 5, setting y = 0 gives x = -5, so it crosses too.
questions.trap: Option D is built to look like option C with x and y swapped, and students who pattern-match on the shape choose it. Reading x = y^2 + 4 at y = 0 gives x = 4, a genuine crossing; what that equation never does is meet the y-axis, which is a different question.

questions.question:
The figure shows the graph of y = |x| - x in the xy-plane.
Column A: the y-coordinate of the point on the graph whose x-coordinate is -5
Column B: the y-coordinate of the point on the graph whose x-coordinate is 5

options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.explanation: Handle the two signs separately. When x is negative, |x| equals -x, so y = -x - x = -2x; at x = -5 that gives y = -2(-5) = 10. When x is positive, |x| equals x, so y = x - x = 0; at x = 5 that gives y = 0. Comparing 10 with 0, Column A is greater. This is why the graph runs flat along the positive x-axis and rises steeply to the left.
questions.trap: Students cancel |x| against x as though the bars did nothing, conclude y = 0 everywhere, and answer C. The bars matter exactly when x is negative, where |x| and x have opposite signs and the expression doubles instead of vanishing.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, a right triangle has its right angle at the origin, and its hypotenuse lies along the line y = 9x - 4. If none of the sides of the triangle is vertical, what is the product of the slopes of the three sides?
questions.explanation: The two legs meet at the right angle at the origin, so they are perpendicular to each other and the product of their slopes is -1. Neither is vertical, so both slopes exist and that product is genuinely defined. The third side is the hypotenuse, which lies along y = 9x - 4 and so has slope 9. Multiplying all three slopes together gives (-1)(9) = -9.
questions.trap: Students hunt for the two leg slopes individually and stall, or they answer 9 by using the hypotenuse alone. The legs never need to be identified: perpendicularity fixes their slope product at -1 regardless of how the triangle is oriented.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, the graph of y = (x^2 + 6)(2x - 7) intersects the x-axis at exactly one point. What is the x-coordinate of that point?
questions.explanation: The graph meets the x-axis where y = 0, and a product is zero only when one of its factors is zero. The first factor, x^2 + 6, is a square plus a positive number, so it is at least 6 for every real x and can never be zero — it contributes no x-intercept at all. That leaves 2x - 7 = 0, which gives x = 7/2 = 3.5, the single crossing point.
questions.trap: Students set x^2 + 6 = 0, move the 6 across and take a square root of -6, producing a spurious answer such as 6 or -6. A sum of a square and a positive constant has no real root, which is exactly why the question can promise only one intersection.
